14.4 Copper, zinc, mercury, silver and iron (with their signature salts)
14.5 Steel: basic oxygen and open hearth; corrosion of iron

html:
Metallurgy is the branch of chemistry that turns a rocky ore into a useful metal, and this chapter carries about four of the fifty Chemistry questions — one of the heaviest inorganic units in the paper.

The questions are of three kinds: a named step with its definition (calcination, roasting, poling, zone refining), a metal with its ore, reagent or characteristic compound (blue vitriol, white vitriol, calomel, corrosive sublimate), and a property of the 3d series explained by electronic configuration or crystal field theory.

Almost every mark here is recall of a name, a formula or a colour, so the tables in this chapter are the part to learn by heart.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The vocabulary of extraction, each with one example: ore, mineral, gangue, flux, slag, concentration, calcination, roasting, smelting, bessemerisation, aluminothermy, electrolytic reduction, poling, electro-refining, zone refining.
  • Calcination = heating without air; roasting = heating in excess air. Slag = flux + gangue; gangue is the impurity, slag is the product that removes it.
  • Sodium by Down's cell (fused NaCl + CaCl₂, graphite anode, iron cathode); NaOH by Castner–Kellner (mercury cathode); Na₂CO₃ by Solvay with the ammonia-recovery loop.
  • The 3d series: configuration, variable oxidation states, colour, paramagnetism, catalysis, alloy formation — and Zn is not a transition metal (d¹⁰ in atom and ion).
  • Crystal field theory: t₂g below eg by Δ₀, high spin when Δ₀ < P, colour from d–d transitions, μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, the spectrochemical series.
  • Copper: roast, smelt, bessemerise, blister copper, electro-refine; blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O. Zinc: blende, roast, reduce with coke; white vitriol ZnSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Mercury from cinnabar through HgO; calomel Hg₂Cl₂ against corrosive sublimate HgCl₂. Silver by cyanide leaching and the Parkes process. Iron in the blast furnace, zone by zone.
  • Steel by the basic oxygen and open-hearth processes; rusting as an electrochemical cell and the four ways to stop it.

14.1 Metallurgical principles

Few metals occur free.

The reactive ones are found as oxides, sulphides, carbonates or silicates, mixed with worthless rock, and the whole business of metallurgy is to separate the metal compound from the rock and then pull the metal out of the compound.

Every extraction, from iron to sodium, follows the same five stages, and the paper tests the name, the purpose and one example of each.

The vocabulary, defined once

Ore, mineral and gangue

A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition and a characteristic crystal structure.

An ore is a mineral (or a mixture of minerals) from which a metal can be extracted profitably — the word "profitably" is part of the definition, which is why bauxite is an ore of aluminium and ordinary clay is not.

The gangue is the unwanted earthy matter — sand, clay, limestone, rock — mixed with the ore.

Flux and slag

A flux is a substance added to the charge to combine with the gangue and form a fusible product. A slag is that fusible product.

The slag melts at a lower temperature than the gangue alone, floats on the molten metal because it is less dense, and protects the metal from re-oxidation by the air.

The choice of flux is fixed by the chemistry of the gangue, and this is the one rule worth memorising:

Gangue Nature Flux used Slag formed
SiO₂ (sand) acidic basic flux: CaO (from limestone) CaSiO₃ (calcium silicate)
CaO or MgO basic acidic flux: SiO₂ (sand) CaSiO₃ or MgSiO₃
FeO basic acidic flux: SiO₂ FeSiO₃
P₂O₅ acidic basic flux: CaO Ca₃(PO₄)₂

Acidic gangue needs a basic flux, and basic gangue needs an acidic flux. The slag must be of the opposite character to the gangue so that the two combine.

Gangue is not slag

Gangue is the impurity that is already in the ore; slag is the new compound made when flux is added to it.

A question that says "the impurity present in an ore is called" wants gangue; one that says "the fusible mass formed by flux and impurity" wants slag. Mixing these two up is the commonest single error in this unit.

Concentration (dressing) of the ore

Concentration is the removal of gangue from the crushed ore. It is a physical separation: the chemical nature of the ore does not change, only its purity.

Method Used for How it works
Hand picking large lumps visible difference in colour or lustre
Washing / levigation oxide ores of Fe, Sn (heavy) gangue is lighter and is washed away in a stream of water
Froth flotation sulphide ores (Cu, Zn, Pb, Ag) powdered ore + water + pine oil (frother) + a collector such as sodium ethyl xanthate; air is blown through. The sulphide particles are wetted by oil, stick to the froth and rise; the gangue is wetted by water and sinks
Magnetic separation ores containing Fe₃O₄ (magnetite), and wolframite the magnetic ore is held by an electromagnet while the non-magnetic gangue falls away
Gravity separation oxide ores the heavier ore settles faster on a shaking Wilfley table
Leaching bauxite (with hot NaOH), Ag and Au (with dilute NaCN) the ore is dissolved selectively in a reagent and recovered from the solution; used when the ore and the gangue differ chemically

Froth flotation is the method the paper asks about most often, and its two-part logic is worth stating: the collector makes the sulphide surface water-repellent, and the frother makes a stable foam that carries those particles to the top.

Depressants and activators (NaCN, CuSO₄) are used to separate one sulphide from another in complex ores.

Calcination and roasting — the two that are always confused

Calcination and roasting

Calcination is the heating of an ore strongly in the absence of air (or in a limited supply of air) to drive off water and carbon dioxide and to decompose the compound.

Roasting is the heating of an ore strongly in excess air so that the ore is oxidised and volatile impurities such as sulphur, arsenic and antimony are removed as their oxides.

Calcination Roasting
Air absent or limited excess
What is removed water of crystallisation, CO₂ S (as SO₂), As, Sb, and carbon
Chemical change decomposition oxidation
Used for carbonates, hydrated oxides sulphide ores
Example CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂
Second example Al₂O₃·2H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 2H₂O 2CuFeS₂ + O₂ → Cu₂S + 2FeS + SO₂

A calcined ore is decomposed; a roasted ore is oxidised. Both leave a metal oxide behind, which is why the next step is the same for both — reduction.

The two exceptions that give the game away
  • Roasting a sulphide produces the oxide plus SO₂ — never the metal directly, and never SO₃ at furnace temperature.
  • Calcination of limestone is the same reaction as the one in a lime kiln, so a question about "the reaction in the zone of slag formation of a blast furnace" is asking about calcination, not roasting.

Reduction: smelting, aluminothermy and electrolysis

Smelting is the reduction of a roasted or calcined ore at high temperature in the presence of a flux, giving molten metal and molten slag. The reducing agent is chosen from the reactivity of the metal:

Method Reducing agent Metals Example
Carbon reduction (smelting) coke, C Zn, Fe, Pb, Sn ZnO + C → Zn + CO
Carbon monoxide CO Fe (blast furnace) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
Aluminothermy (thermite) Al powder Cr, Mn, Fe, and metals whose oxides are very stable Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Cr + Al₂O₃
Hydrogen reduction H₂ W, Mo WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O
Electrolytic reduction electric current Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al (very reactive) 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂
Self-reduction the ore itself Cu, Pb Cu₂S + 2Cu₂O → 6Cu + SO₂
Displacement a more reactive metal Ag, Au 2Na[Ag(CN)₂] + Zn → 2Ag + Na₂[Zn(CN)₄]

Aluminothermy (the Goldschmidt process) works because aluminium has a very high affinity for oxygen: the reaction is so exothermic that the temperature rises above 2000 °C and the metal comes out molten.

The mixture of Fe₂O₃ and Al is the thermite used to weld railway tracks.

Metals low in the electrochemical series (Cu, Ag, Au, Hg) can be obtained by heating their oxides alone; metals high in the series (Na, Mg, Al) can only be obtained by electrolysis of a fused salt, because no chemical reducing agent is strong enough.

Refining

Method Principle Metal
Liquation the metal has a lower melting point than its impurities and is allowed to flow away Sn, Pb, Bi
Distillation the metal is volatile Zn, Hg, Cd
Poling molten metal is stirred with green wood; the gases (CH₄, CO) reduce the oxide back to metal Cu (blister copper)
Cupellation the impurity is oxidised and absorbed by a bone-ash cupel Ag (from Pb)
Electro-refining impure metal is the anode, pure metal the cathode; metal dissolves and redeposits Cu, Zn, Ag, Al, Ni
Zone refining a molten zone is moved slowly along a rod; impurities stay in the melt and are swept to one end Si, Ge (semiconductor grade)
Vapour phase (Mond) the metal forms a volatile compound which is decomposed elsewhere Ni: Ni + 4CO → Ni(CO)₄ at 60 °C, decomposed at 180 °C

Electro-refining of copper uses the impure blister copper as the anode, a thin sheet of pure copper as the cathode, and acidified copper sulphate as the electrolyte.

Copper dissolves from the anode, migrates as Cu²⁺ and deposits on the cathode at 99.95 % purity; less active impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) fall as anode mud and are recovered, while more active ones (Fe, Ni, Zn) stay in solution.

Zone refining relies on the fact that an impurity is more soluble in the melt than in the solid: the molten zone carries the impurity along and leaves pure crystal behind it, and repeating the pass gives the 99.9999999 % silicon needed for chips.

Lime for an acidic gangue

Problem. A copper charge contains 120 kg of ore that is 10 % SiO₂ by mass. How much limestone, 90 % pure CaCO₃, must be added to remove all the silica as slag? (Ca = 40, Si = 28, O = 16, C = 12)

Solution. Mass of SiO₂ = 0.10 × 120 = 12 kg = 12/60 = 0.20 kmol. CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃, so 0.20 kmol of CaO is needed = 0.20 × 56 = 11.2 kg. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, so CaCO₃ needed = 0.20 × 100 = 20.0 kg. At 90 % purity: 20.0/0.90 = 22.2 kg of limestone.

14.2 Alkali and alkaline-earth metals; sodium, sodium hydroxide and sodium carbonate

Occurrence and the trends down the group

The alkali metals (group 1: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) have the configuration ns¹ and the alkaline-earth metals (group 2: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) have ns². Both are so reactive that they are never found free.

Metal Chief minerals
Na rock salt NaCl, Chile saltpetre NaNO₃, borax Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O, feldspar
K sylvine KCl, carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, saltpetre KNO₃
Mg magnesite MgCO₃, dolomite CaCO₃·MgCO₃, carnallite, sea water
Ca limestone CaCO₃, gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O, fluorspar CaF₂, apatite

Trends down group 1. Atomic and ionic radius increase, ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease, metallic character and reactivity increase, melting point decreases (Li 180 °C to Cs 28.5 °C, because the atoms are held by weaker metallic bonding as the size grows), density generally increases (Li 0.53 to Cs 1.87 g cm⁻³, with potassium lighter than sodium as the one exception), and the hydration enthalpy of the ion decreases — Li⁺ is the most heavily hydrated and therefore has the largest hydrated radius but the highest hydration energy.

Trends down group 2. The same fall in ionisation energy and rise in reactivity, but the group is harder, denser and much less reactive than group 1 because of the extra nuclear charge and the pair of electrons. Two solubility trends are examined:

  • Hydroxides become more soluble down the group: Be(OH)₂ is insoluble and amphoteric, Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, Ca(OH)₂ is fairly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ is very soluble.
  • Sulphates and carbonates become less soluble down the group, and the thermal stability of the carbonates increases down the group, because the larger cation polarises the carbonate ion less.

Chemical character. Sodium reacts vigorously with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. It burns in air to the monoxide and, on strong heating, to the peroxide Na₂O₂.

It dissolves in liquid ammonia to give a deep blue solution of solvated electrons, which is a strong reducing agent. Sodium is stored under kerosene because it would otherwise react with the moisture and oxygen of the air.

Calcium reacts with cold water more gently than sodium (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂), magnesium only with hot water or steam (Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂), and beryllium not at all. Oxides: BeO and Al₂O₃ are amphoteric, MgO and CaO are basic.

Flame colours are worth a line each: Li crimson, Na golden yellow, K lilac, Rb red-violet, Cs blue; Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green. Sodium street lamps are yellow for this reason.

Sodium by Down's cell

Sodium cannot be reduced by carbon or aluminium — it is too reactive — so it is made by electrolysis of fused sodium chloride.

The melting point of pure NaCl is 801 °C, too high to work comfortably, so about 40 % calcium chloride is added: the mixture melts near 600 °C and the CaCl₂ also lowers the solubility of the metal in the melt.

  • Anode: graphite (carbon), at the centre. Chlorine is liberated: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
  • Cathode: a ring of iron gauze around the anode. Sodium is deposited: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.
  • The bell above the cathode collects the molten sodium, which is less dense than the melt and floats up; the chlorine is drawn off from the central hood. The two products must be kept apart, or they recombine.

\text{2NaCl (fused)} \rightarrow \text{2Na} + \text{Cl}_2

Uses of sodium: as a coolant in fast-breeder nuclear reactors (it has a low melting point and a high heat capacity), in sodium-vapour lamps, in the manufacture of Na₂O₂, NaCN and sodium amalgam, and as a reducing agent in organic chemistry.

Sodium hydroxide — the Castner–Kellner process

Castner–Kellner electrolyses concentrated brine with a flowing mercury cathode and a graphite anode.

Sodium is discharged at the mercury in preference to hydrogen because of the high overvoltage of hydrogen on mercury, and it dissolves to form sodium amalgam. The amalgam is run into a separate decomposer where water oxidises it:

  • At the mercury cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (dissolves in Hg).
  • At the graphite anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
  • In the decomposer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

\text{2NaCl} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2NaOH} + \text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2

The mercury is pumped back, so it is a continuous process, and the NaOH produced is very pure and free of chloride.

The older diaphragm cell and the modern membrane cell do the same overall reaction without mercury; the membrane cell avoids both the mercury hazard and the asbestos diaphragm, and is what new plants build.

Properties and uses. NaOH is a white, deliquescent solid that absorbs CO₂ from the air (2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O) and dissolves in water with a large release of heat.

It is used in soap making (saponification of fats), in paper and textile processing, in rayon, in petroleum refining, in the extraction of alumina from bauxite, and as a drain cleaner.

Sodium carbonate — the Solvay (ammonia–soda) process

Solvay's genius was to use a cheap, recyclable base (ammonia) to make an insoluble salt (sodium bicarbonate) precipitate out of brine, and then to recover the ammonia with lime. Five steps, and every equation is examinable.

Step 1 — carbon dioxide and lime. Limestone is calcined in a kiln: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The CO₂ goes to the carbonating tower; the CaO is slaked: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, and the milk of lime goes to the ammonia-recovery tower.

Step 2 — brine saturated with ammonia. Purified brine is saturated with NH₃ in an absorption tower. The ammonia makes the solution alkaline, which is what allows it to absorb CO₂ in quantity.

Step 3 — carbonation. CO₂ is bubbled through the ammoniated brine under pressure: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl.

Sodium bicarbonate is only sparingly soluble, and the presence of NH₄Cl and unchanged NaCl (the common-ion effect) pushes it out of solution almost completely. It is filtered off.

Step 4 — calcination of the bicarbonate. 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O. The CO₂ is returned to step 3, so no carbon dioxide is wasted.

Step 5 — ammonia recovery. The filtrate contains NH₄Cl. It is heated with milk of lime: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NH₃ + CaCl₂ + 2H₂O, and the ammonia is returned to step 2.

This loop is what makes the process economic: the only raw materials consumed are brine and limestone, and the only waste is calcium chloride.

Overall: CaCO₃ + 2NaCl → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂.

Properties and uses. Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (soda ash) is a white powder; the decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is washing soda, which effloresces in dry air.

It is used in glass making, soap and detergent manufacture, water softening (it precipitates Ca²⁺ as CaCO₃), paper making, and in the laboratory as a primary standard for acids. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

Why Solvay cannot make potassium carbonate

The process depends on NaHCO₃ being sparingly soluble so that it crystallises out.

Potassium bicarbonate is much more soluble, so it never precipitates and the ammonia-soda route fails for K₂CO₃ — potassium carbonate is still made from wood ash or by the carbonation of KOH.

Soda ash from brine

Problem. A Solvay plant treats 585 kg of pure NaCl a day with excess limestone and ammonia, and the overall yield of Na₂CO₃ is 80 %. What mass of soda ash is obtained? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5, C = 12, O = 16)

Solution. NaCl = 585/58.5 = 10 kmol. From CaCO₃ + 2NaCl → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂, 2 mol NaCl give 1 mol Na₂CO₃, so 10 kmol NaCl give 5 kmol Na₂CO₃. Mass = 5 × 106 = 530 kg at 100 %; at 80 %: 530 × 0.80 = 424 kg.

14.3 3d transition metals: complex shapes and crystal field theory

A transition metal has an incomplete d subshell in some common oxidation state (Sc → Zn across the 3d row; Zn, with only d¹⁰ Zn²⁺, sits on the honorary bench).

The nearness of 4s and 3d energies yields the family's party tricks: variable oxidation states (Mn: +2 to +7), coloured compounds, paramagnetism (unpaired d electrons, counted by the spin-only moment \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} BM conceptually), catalysis (empty d orbitals and easy redox swapping), and a passion for complex ions — a central metal accepting lone pairs from ligands (NH₃, H₂O, Cl⁻, CN⁻, en…; chelating ligands like EDTA grip with several teeth — and are used clinically to drag Pb²⁺ out of poisoned patients, Ch. 15).

Coordination no. Geometry Familiar examples
2 linear [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Tollens'), [AuCl₂]⁻
4 tetrahedral [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺, [NiCl₄]²⁻, [FeCl₄]⁻
4 square planar [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin — the cis form is the anticancer drug; geometry is destiny)
6 octahedral [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺, haem's Fe

Crystal field theory treats ligands as point charges approaching the metal.

In an octahedral complex they march down the x, y, z axes — straight at the d_{z^2} and d_{x^2-y^2} orbitals (e_g, repelled upward) while d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{zx} point between the axes (t₂g, sheltered, lower).

The gap is Δo, sized by the ligand (spectrochemical series: I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O < NH₃, en < CN⁻, CO), the metal's oxidation state and row.

Electrons then face a rent-vs-roommates decision: if Δo is small (weak field), they spread out obeying Hund (high spin, e.g. [FeF₆]³⁻ d⁵ all unpaired); if Δo is large (strong field), they pair up in t₂g first (low spin, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ with one unpaired).

Absorbing a photon of energy Δo promotes an electron t₂g → e_g: the absorbed colour is removed and the complementary colour is seen (red absorbed → blue-green observed, as in Cu²⁺'s aqua complex; d⁰ Sc³⁺ and d¹⁰ Zn²⁺ have no d–d moves and stay colourless).

14.4 Copper, zinc, mercury, silver and iron (with their signature salts)

Copper — chief ore copper pyrites/chalcopyrite CuFeS₂ (also cuprite Cu₂O, malachite CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂, azurite).

Froth-float, roast gently (only part-oxidize), smelt to a matte of Cu₂S + FeS, slag off Fe as FeSiO₃, bessemerize to blister copper, electrorefine (acidsulphate bath: impure anode dissolves, pure Cu plates the cathode; Ag, Au, Pt drop as valuable anode mud; more reactive impurities stay in solution).

The metal is the wiring/coinage standard (alloys brass Cu–Zn, bronze Cu–Sn).

Blue vitriol, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is the signature salt: deep blue crystals (4 waters coordinate Cu²⁺, the 5th is H-bonded) turning white on heating as the anhydrous salt forms — the classic test for water; with lime it makes Bordeaux mixture, the vineyards' fungicide; Fehling's solution uses its tartrate complex to detect reducing sugars (Ch. 19).

In moist air copper slowly coats with green basic carbonate — the skin of old roofs and temple bells.

Zinc — ores zinc blende ZnS and calamine ZnCO₃. Roast/calcine to ZnO, reduce with coke at ~1400 K; zinc (b.p. 1180 K) leaves as vapour and is condensed (a built-in distillation refining; care to stop it reoxidizing).

Amphoteric like Al (Zn + 2NaOH (hot) → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂), it galvanizes iron (sacrificial coat, Ch. 10) and fills dry cells (the can is the anode).

White vitriol, ZnSO₄·7H₂O, is its colourless everyday salt; ZnO is "philosopher's wool" (from burning Zn) and calamine lotion's ZnO/Fe₂O₃ is a first-aid-box citizen.

Mercury — from cinnabar HgS, which merely roasts in air: HgS + O₂ → Hg + SO₂ (the oxide first formed also self-reduces: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂ when hot).

The liquid metal (m.p. −39 °C, vapour poisonous) amalgamates most metals (not iron — hence iron flasks), fills thermometers and barometers (retreating, post-Minamata conventions — Ch. 15).

Two chlorides must never be confused: calomel, Hg₂Cl₂ — white, Hg(I) — with NH₄OH turns black (HgNH₂Cl + Hg), the test for Hg₂²⁺; and corrosive sublimate, HgCl₂ — Hg(II), violently poisonous protein coagulant (albumen is the antidote: milk/egg-white give it innocent protein to curdle), whose solution with excess KI gives the Nessler complex (K₂[HgI₄]).

Silver — native and as argentite Ag₂S; extracted by the cyanide process: Ag₂S + 4NaCN ⇌ 2Na[Ag(CN)₂] + Na₂S (air oxidizes the sulphide on), then zinc dust displaces the metal: 2Na[Ag(CN)₂] + Zn → Na₂[Zn(CN)₄] + 2Ag↓.

Best electrical conductor of all metals; untarnished by air alone but blackened by trace H₂S (Ag₂S film); AgNO₃ (lunar caustic) blackens skin (to Ag) and with halides gives the Ch. 13 precipitates; AgBr emulsions powered a century of photography (light → Ag nuclei → developer amplifies).

Iron — ores haematite Fe₂O₃ (chief), magnetite Fe₃O₄, siderite FeCO₃, iron pyrites FeS₂ (usually left for its sulphur).

The blast furnace is charged with ore + coke + limestone; descending solids meet rising heat: coke burns at the tuyères (≈ 2000 K), CO forms (C + CO₂ ⇌ 2CO) and does the reducing upstairs (Fe₂O₃ → Fe₃O₄ → FeO → Fe), limestone calcines and its CaO fluxes silica to a molten CaSiO₃ slag floating on the iron.

Out flows pig iron (~4 % C plus Si, Mn, P, S — hard, brittle, low-melting) much of it cast directly (cast iron, ~3 % C) or converted: wrought iron (pig iron's carbon burnt out in a puddling furnace — the purest, softest, weldable form) and steel (0.1–1.5 % C, tuned by alloying).

14.5 Steel: basic oxygen and open hearth; corrosion of iron

Basic oxygen process (LD) Open-hearth (Siemens–Martin)
Charge ~70 % molten pig iron + scrap, lime flux pig iron + scrap + ore, any proportions
Heat source oxidation itself — a water-cooled lance blows pure O₂ onto the melt (no fuel) producer-gas flames over a shallow hearth, regenerative chequer-work recycles waste heat
Chemistry C → CO/CO₂; Si, Mn, P oxidized into the basic slag (CaO-rich lining grabs P as calcium phosphate) same oxidation, slower and sampled as it goes
Time/control ~20–30 min per heat, huge tonnage, less mid-course correction 6–10 hours, analysis before tapping — the quality-control classic, now largely superseded
Nitrogen low (pure O₂: no air N₂) — better than old Bessemer (air-blown: brittle nitrided steel) moderate

Corrosion (rusting) is an electrochemical duet (Ch. 10) needing water and oxygen (both — the classic three-tube school proof): at anodic spots Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; at cathodic spots O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; the Fe²⁺ is further oxidized by air to hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, the flaky, non-protective rust (in the dry-salt air of the Terai winter and the monsoon's wet both electrolytes and O₂ abound).

Salts accelerate (conductivity), acid rain too; attached nobler metals (Cu rivets) create ruthless local cells.

Defences: barrier coats (paint, oil, plastic, tin plate — works only until scratched, whereupon Fe, the baser metal, rusts faster), galvanizing (Zn is baser still: it corrodes sacrificially and protects even at scratches — the tin/zinc contrast is a perennial question), cathodic protection with Mg blocks on pipelines and hulls, alloying (stainless steel's Cr₂O₃ skin), and keeping the metal dry/earthed in design.

Worked example 14.1 — following electrons in refining

Problem. In copper electrorefining a current is passed for 10 hours depositing 3.175 kg of pure copper at the cathode.(a) Average current used (F = 96 500 C).(b) What happens to the Ag and Fe impurities in the anode?

Solution.(a) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu: moles = 3175/63.5 = 50 mol ⇒ 100 F of charge = 9.65×10⁶ C over 36 000 s ⇒ I = 268 A (refineries do indeed run hundreds of amps per cell, many cells in series).(b) Silver (and Au, Pt) — nobler than Cu — never ionizes: as the anode dissolves around it, it simply falls as anode mud (recovered eagerly). Iron/zinc, baser than copper, ionize but their ions lose the discharge race to Cu²⁺ at the cathode and accumulate in the electrolyte — icily obedient to Ch. 10's series.

Tin plate vs galvanized iron at a scratch

Tin is nobler than iron: a pinhole in tinplate makes the exposed iron the anode of a cell and rusting accelerates there. Zinc is baser: a scratch in galvanizing sacrifices the surrounding zinc and the iron stays cathodic and safe. One sentence, one recurring mark.

Water out of blue vitriol

Problem. 25.0 g of blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O (M = 250) is heated until constant mass at ~230 °C. What mass of white residue remains, and what mass of water left?

Solution. Moles of vitriol = 25.0/250 = 0.1 mol; each mole carries one mole of CuSO₄ (M = 160) and five of water. Residue = 0.1 × 160 = 16.0 g of anhydrous CuSO₄; water lost = 0.5 × 18 = 9.0 g.

The blue that leaves is the water of crystallisation holding the copper's d–d colour — anhydrous CuSO₄ is white until a drop of water returns the blue, the classic test for water itself.

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Must-know
Sequence concentrate → calcine/roast → reduce (ladder: roast < carbon < electrolysis) → refine
Special words gangue, flux, slag; matte (Cu₂S/FeS); blister Cu; anode mud; oleum-adjacent: cryolite for Al
Named rigs froth flotation (sulphides, NaCN depressant); Bayer (bauxite); Downs (Na); Hall–Héroult (Al); Bessemer converter (Cu self-reduction); zone refining (Si/Ge)
s-block flames (Na yellow); Downs Na; chlor-alkali NaOH; Solvay Na₂CO₃ (KHCO₃ too soluble for K); lime cycle; PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O
Complexes CN 6 octahedral / 4 tetrahedral / 4 square planar (cisplatin!) / 2 linear; t₂g–eg split Δo; strong field = low spin
Big five metals Cu blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O⇌white; Zn white vitriol, distils, galvanizes; Hg calomel vs corrosive sublimate; Ag cyanide process; Fe blast furnace
Steel & rust LD (O₂ lance, 30 min) vs open hearth (slow, sampled); rust Fe₂O₃·xH₂O needs O₂+H₂O; Zn sacrificial, Sn only a barrier

Chapter summary

  • Ores are concentrated (flotation owns the sulphides), converted to oxides (calcination without air, roasting with it), then reduced by the cheapest agent the Ellingham ladder allows — carbon for the middle class, electricity for the aristocrats, self-reduction for copper and mercury.
  • Refining polishes with green poles, electric baths and moving molten zones; impurities are sorted by the same electrochemical series that runs the cells.
  • The s-block supplies sodium's industrial trio (metal, hydroxide, carbonate) by Downs, chlor-alkali and Solvay routes, and calcium's lime cycle closes on itself.
  • Transition metals wear complexes whose colours, spins and geometries crystal-field splitting predicts — from tetraammine blue to chemotherapy's cisplatin.
  • Iron's blast furnace and the two steel converters turn carbon content into a dial (pig ≫ cast > steel > wrought), while rust — a wet electrochemical cell — is fought by smarter neighbours: zinc above all.

1. (c) — the Ellingham verdict: C could reduce Al₂O₃ only above ~2000 °C (and then makes Al₄C₃). Electrolysis is the practical road.

4. (b) — the entire Solvay economy hangs on NaHCO₃'s modest solubility; KHCO₃ stays in solution and nothing crystallizes out.

8. (a) — Ch. 10's series doing neighbourhood watch: Fe is between Zn and Sn.

9. (b) — nobility here is a refusal to ionize: the copper dissolves around them and gravity collects the fee.

10. (a) — ΔH ≈ −850 kJ per equation, enough to pour white-hot iron directly into a rail joint.

11. (d) — the impurities are the fuel; scrap is even added as a coolant.

12. (c) — elemental Hg vapour crosses lung and blood–brain barriers, and aquatic bacteria convert spills to methylmercury, the food-chain concentrating poison of Minamata Bay.

15. (b) — chelation therapy: six-toothed EDTA wraps Pb²⁺, and the kidney can evict the parcel (CaNa₂EDTA is the clinical salt, so the body's Ca²⁺ is not stripped).

Model answer D1: general principles of metallurgy (10 marks)

Introduction. A mineral is a natural compound of a metal, and an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably. Metallurgy is the whole process of getting a pure metal from its ore.

Steps.

  1. Crushing and concentration (dressing) removes the gangue. - Gravity separation (hydraulic washing) for heavy oxide ores such as haematite and cassiterite. - Froth flotation for sulphide ores (galena, zinc blende). Pine oil makes the ore particles float in the froth and the gangue settles. Depressants such as NaCN separate ZnS from PbS. - Magnetic separation for magnetic ores (magnetite, wolframite and cassiterite). - Leaching for chemical separation, for example bauxite with NaOH (Bayer's process).
  2. Conversion to oxide. - Calcination: heating in limited or no air, for carbonates and hydrated ores, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. - Roasting: heating in excess air, for sulphides, 2\text{ZnS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{ZnO} + 2\text{SO}_2.
  3. Reduction with carbon (smelting), carbon monoxide, hydrogen, aluminium (thermite, aluminothermy), or electrolysis for reactive metals (Na, Al, Mg).
  4. Refining. Liquation (Sn, Pb), distillation (Zn, Hg), electrolytic refining (Cu, Ag, Au, Al), zone refining (Si, Ge, Ga for semiconductors), vapour-phase refining (Mond's process for Ni, van Arkel for Zr, Ti) and chromatography.

Flux and slag. A flux combines with the gangue to give a fusible slag: CaO (basic flux) for acidic gangue SiO₂, giving CaSiO₃, and SiO₂ for basic gangue.

Ellingham diagram. The plot of \Delta G^{\circ} against T for the formation of oxides. A metal whose line lies lower can reduce the oxide of a metal whose line is higher at that temperature, so Al reduces Cr₂O₃ and Fe₂O₃.

The line for 2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO} slopes downward, so above about 710^{\circ}\text{C} carbon can reduce FeO, and above about 1000^{\circ}\text{C} ZnO.

Method Example Reason
Reduction by carbon Zn, Fe, Sn cheap and the oxide line is above CO
Electrolysis Na, Mg, Al very strong affinity for oxygen
Self-reduction Cu, Pb, Hg from sulphide \text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} \to 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2
Hydrometallurgy Au, Ag (cyanide leaching) 4\text{Au} + 8\text{CN}^- + \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4[\text{Au(CN)}_2]^- + 4\text{OH}^-, then displacement by Zn

Numerical. To make 1\ \text{tonne} of iron from haematite (Fe₂O₃, 160\ \text{g mol}^{-1}): 112\ \text{g} of Fe comes from 160\ \text{g} of Fe₂O₃, so 1000\ \text{kg} of Fe needs 1429\ \text{kg} of pure Fe₂O₃, or 2041\ \text{kg} of ore that is 70\% pure.

Conclusion. The method of reduction is chosen from the position of the metal in the electrochemical and Ellingham series: the more reactive the metal, the more powerful the reduction needed.

Model answer D2: extraction of aluminium and iron (10 marks)

Introduction. Aluminium (from bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O) is extracted by electrolysis and iron (from haematite) by carbon reduction.

Aluminium: purification (Bayer's process). Bauxite is heated with concentrated NaOH, which dissolves alumina as sodium aluminate: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄]. Fe₂O₃ and SiO₂ remain as red mud.

The filtrate is seeded with Al(OH)₃ and gives pure Al(OH)₃, which is heated to Al₂O₃.

Hall-Héroult electrolysis. Pure alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) with fluorspar (CaF₂). Cryolite lowers the melting point from 2050^{\circ}\text{C} to about 950^{\circ}\text{C} and raises the conductivity.

A steel tank lined with carbon is the cathode and graphite rods are the anodes.

  • Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (liquid, tapped from the bottom).
  • Anode: 2\text{O}^{2-} \to \text{O}_2 + 4\text{e}^- and the oxygen burns the anode to CO and CO₂, so the anodes are replaced regularly.

Iron: blast furnace. The charge of haematite, coke and limestone is fed from the top and hot air is blown in from the bottom.

Zone (top to bottom) Temperature Reaction
Combustion about 1900 K \text{C} + \text{O}_2 \to \text{CO}_2, then \text{CO}_2 + \text{C} \to 2\text{CO}
Reduction 500 to 900 K \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{CO} \to 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2 (upper part gives \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4 and FeO)
Slag formation 1000 to 1500 K \text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2, \text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{CaSiO}_3
Fusion about 1500 K molten iron and slag collect below

The product is pig iron (about 4\% C), which is converted to cast iron, wrought iron (almost pure) or steel (by the basic oxygen process).

Iron type Carbon
Wrought iron 0.1 to 0.25\%
Steel 0.25 to 2\%
Cast iron 2 to 4.5\%

Alloys: stainless steel (Fe, Cr, Ni), duralumin (Al, Cu, Mg, Mn), brass (Cu, Zn), bronze (Cu, Sn).

Numerical. To produce 1\ \text{kg} of Al: \dfrac{1000}{27} = 37.0\ \text{mol} needs 3\times37.0 = 111\ \text{mol} of electrons, so the charge is 111\times96\,500 = 1.07\times10^7\ \text{C}.

At 4\ \text{V} the energy is 4.3\times10^7\ \text{J}, about 11.9\ \text{kWh} at least. This is why aluminium smelters need cheap electricity.

Conclusion. Aluminium needs electrolysis in molten cryolite because carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃, while iron is reduced by CO in the blast furnace.
